account: On 12 October 2023 the Vesuvius Challenge announced that contestant Luke Farritor, a 21-year-old student, had read ΠΟΡΦΥΡΑϹ (“purple”) inside the unopened Herculaneum scroll PHerc.Paris.4. He used a machine-learning model trained on the “crackle” pattern of ink visible in X-ray computed tomography (CT) scans. On 5 February 2024 the organizers gave the $700,000 grand prize to Youssef Nader, Luke Farritor and Julian Schilliger. Their TimeSformer-based ink-detection models recovered 15 columns and more than 2,000 characters of Greek text. Papyrologists Federica Nicolardi, Richard Janko and Robert Fowler reviewed the passages, which discuss pleasure, food and music and are probably by Philodemus. The University of Kentucky, whose virtual-unwrapping software underlies the contest, called the result a new, readable Herculaneum text.

ai_role.statement: The contestants' ink-detection models produced the ink images from which papyrologists read the text. The ink is not visible in the raw CT data. Virtual unwrapping (non-AI) was a necessary precondition. The readings were validated by an independent papyrological review organized by the contest.

later.note: The same AI ink-detection approach was applied to a second scroll, PHerc. 172 at the Bodleian, scanned at Diamond Light Source in July 2024, yielding columns of text including the word διατροπή.
later.quote: One of the first words to be translated was the Ancient Greek διατροπή meaning 'disgust', which appears twice within a few columns of text. Since the scroll was scanned at the Diamond Light Source in Harwell in July 2024, the UK's national synchrotron science facility, the Vesuvius Challenge team have worked with AI to piece together the images and enhance the clarity of the text.

fields.account: On 12 October 2023 the Vesuvius Challenge announced that contestant Luke Farritor, a 21-year-old student, had read ΠΟΡΦΥΡΑϹ (“purple”) inside the unopened Herculaneum scroll PHerc.Paris.4. He used a machine-learning model trained on the “crackle” pattern of ink visible in X-ray computed tomography (CT) scans. On 5 February 2024 the organizers gave the $700,000 grand prize to Youssef Nader, Luke Farritor and Julian Schilliger. Their TimeSformer-based ink-detection models recovered 15 columns and more than 2,000 characters of Greek text. Papyrologists Federica Nicolardi, Richard Janko and Robert Fowler reviewed the passages, which discuss pleasure, food and music and are probably by Philodemus. The University of Kentucky, whose virtual-unwrapping software underlies the contest, called the result a new, readable Herculaneum text.
